name: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (Flathead Reservation)
land_summary: The 1855 Hellgate Treaty set aside the Flathead Reservation for the Bitterroot Salish, Upper Pend d'Oreille and Kootenai, carved from homelands that once reached across western Montana and beyond. The negotiations were poorly translated, and tribal leaders came away understanding the reservation to be larger than its written boundary. Salish families who had stayed in the Bitterroot Valley were forced north to the reservation in 1891. Over strong tribal objection, a 1904 federal law split the reservation into individual allotments and declared the rest surplus. Homesteaders followed, and more than half a million acres passed out of tribal hands. Since the 1930s the Tribes have bought much of that land back, and in 2020 Congress restored the former National Bison Range to them. Today the reservation covers about 1.3 million acres, including the southern half of Flathead Lake, in a checkerboard of tribal, individual and private ownership.
homelands: The Tribes describe their homelands as covering all of western Montana and reaching into parts of Idaho, British Columbia and Wyoming. Their Salish-Pend d'Oreille Culture Committee writes that Salish bands lived on both sides of the Continental Divide, from the upper Missouri headwaters valleys west to the Big Hole and Bitterroot valleys, and that Pend d'Oreille bands lived along the Flathead, Clark Fork and Pend Oreille river systems into northern Idaho and eastern Washington.

timeline.event: The Hellgate Treaty sets aside the Flathead Reservation for the Salish, Pend d'Oreille and Kootenai.
The federal government forcibly removes the remaining Salish from the Bitterroot Valley to the reservation.
Congress passes the Flathead Allotment Act, dividing the reservation and providing for the sale of surplus land.
Congress restores the National Bison Range, created on tribal land without the Tribes' consent, to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes.

notes: Disputed: tribal leaders understood the 1855 reservation to be larger than the treaty's written description (OPI), and the Tribes hold that the 1904 act broke the treaty's promise of exclusive use. Only OPI documents the 1971 Court of Claims finding that the opening breached the treaty, so the summary does not include it. The 1910 homestead opening is supported by OPI alone, so the summary leaves it undated. The Bison Range's founding is 1908 on bisonrange.org and 1909 in OPI, so that event is undated and left out of the summary. OPI says President Theodore Roosevelt signed the 1904 Flathead Allotment Act. The statute shows it was approved April 23, 1904, but does not name the signer, so there is only one explicit source and T.R. is not mentioned. The 2015 acquisition of Kerr Dam (now Séliš Ksanka Qlispé Dam) is single-source (cskt.org) and left out. Flathead Lake: I could not confirm on a CSKT-published page that the Tribes name it sacred (cskt.org is behind Cloudflare and could not be read directly), so sacred_places is empty. The Culture Committee page gives the Salish name for the lake and says it was the center of a Pend d'Oreille band. Reviewers can add it from a CSKT source. Acreage: cskt.org gives about 1.3 million acres and the Governor's Office about 1.2 million.
